whole_row.py:135 builds {id(scope.expression): scope} from traverse_scope(statement); :154-155 looks up id(nearest ancestor exp.Select). In installed sqlglot scope.py, Scope.__init__ sets self.expression = expression (l.115); _traverse_scope dispatches exp.Select to _traverse_select and yields the scope (l.724-725, 793). Child scopes are created via Scope.branch, which uses expression.unnest() (l.173), so derived-table/subquery wrappers (exp.Subquery) are unwrapped to the inner Select; set-operation operands likewise go through branch. Hence each Select gets a scope keyed by that Select node. Cases where no scope is keyed (e.g. UDTF/DML wrapper roots) fall to the code's fail-closed 'scope is None -> return True' (l.156-158), so the claim's lookup is sound. Rejections lines do not bear on this claim.

_uses_table_shorthand (whole_row.py:112-124) uses statement.find_all(exp.Identifier), so it covers every nested subquery and statement (called from _whole_row_reference, line 104, for each statement). The only allowed cases are the exemptions the docstring itself lists: COUNT, EXISTS, query or UDTF scopes, table-valued functions, catalogs. I found no counterexample to the claim, but I did not run the code against sqlglot, so the sqlglot scope behavior is read from the guard's logic and not tested. The rejections lines concern other matters and do not affect this claim.
